articles.title: Check Out the National High School Law Review, Vol. II
articles.content:
由Studium项目发起的全国高中法律评论期刊第二卷已经出版。该项目的宪法法律顾问委员会由全美宪法中心首席执行官杰弗里·罗森教授、前美国公民自由联盟主席娜丁·斯特罗森教授、前首席法官戴安·伍德教授、法官道格·金斯堡教授和亚当·怀特教授等专家组成。

以下是创始人奥利维亚·伊芙·格罗斯在卷首语中的致辞：

我们怀着极大的自豪感向各位介绍本年度的全国高中法律评论期刊。每一卷不仅是论文的集合，更代表着一个不断壮大的全国范围内的学生和教育工作者社区。他们致力于研究宪法法律，认真对待彼此的观点，并培养负责任的公民行为习惯。

从最初一个简单的信念——学生应有机会直接探讨国家最重要的法律问题——发展到如今的全国性运动，我们格外自豪地看到这场运动正扩展到新的学校、新的州和新的课堂，让数千名学生加入以证据、理性和相互尊重为基础的对话中。

高中法律评论的存在是为了给学生提供一个真正的思考、写作和发表的平台。通过仔细研读最高法院判决、持续的课堂讨论以及发表自己的法律文章，学生学会精确分析论点、清楚表达观点，并运用宪法推理进行令人愉悦的辩论。这些不仅仅是学术技能，更是为学生们准备参与公民生活的习惯。

这一工作的核心是令人愉悦的辩论实践。学生不仅被挑战要捍卫自己的结论，还要理解与自己不同的观点的最强版本。他们学会将想法与身份分开，质疑自己的假设，并认识到，在好奇和慷慨的态度下，分歧不仅不会削弱，反而会加强一个学习者社区。本卷收录的论文体现了这一承诺，展示了谨慎的推理、真诚的探究，以及勇于以信念和尊重面对困难问题的意愿。

没有每天在课堂上使这项工作对学生可及的杰出教育工作者，这一切都不可能实现。教师们创造了条件，让学生愿意提出棘手的问题，修正自己的想法，并以严谨和温和的态度相互交流。他们的领导力使宪法法律从需要研究的原始资料转变为需要实践的生活方式，我们深感感激他们的合作。

随着社区的持续壮大，本刊的意义也越来越深远。来自全国各地的学生现在共同贡献作品，阅读和学习那些经历、观点和社区与自己大不相同的同龄人的见解。全国高中法律评论已经不仅是一本年度期刊，更成为了一个全国性的论坛，年轻人在这里发现，有意义的分歧可以成为学习的动力，而非分裂的源头。

向所有在本期刊中发表作品的学生致以祝贺。你们愿意仔细思考、深入写作并分享想法，为比一篇法律论文更宏大的事业作出了贡献。向所有使本期刊出版成为可能的教师、学校和分会致以感谢，感谢你们相信这项工作的重要性，并帮助这个社区继续成长。

我们对这场运动取得的成就感到振奋，更对其未来的发展充满期待。我们希望这期期刊能激励更多学校加入我们，共同培养一代懂得如何以理性、尊重和开放的心态进行辩论的公民。

（原文发布于Reason.com，标题为《Check Out the National High School Law Review, Vol. II》）
articles.summary:
It's a project of Studium; Studium's Constitutional Law Advisory Board includes Prof. and National Constitution Center CEO Jeffrey Rosen, Prof. and former ACLU President Nadine Strossen, Prof. and former Chief Judge Diane Wood, Prof. and Judge Doug Ginsburg, and Prof. Adam White. Volume II is now out, and it contains these articles:

  1. Sebastian Lewin, The Unassailable Theory of Liberty
  2. Eileen Wang, ICWA's Dual Purpose After Haaland v. Brackeen: Reading Alito's Dissent Alongside Gorsuch's Concurrence
  3. Steele Barhydt, On Tyranny
  4. Anna Yuras & Piper Schmitz, Why Originalism Should Prevail as the Dominant Method of Interpretation
  5. Benjamin Berer, Counterman v. Colorado: Why the Recklessness Standard Fails Victims of Online Threats
  6. Morgan Cole, Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo in the Upside Down: How a Fight Over Fishery Salaries Could Spark an Unintentional Sanctuary for Science
  7. Adam Watson, A Campaign Finance System Which Doesn't Work
  8. Michelle Wang & Colomba Joulin-Batejat, Burden and Constitutional Risk in Glossip v. Gross
  9. Alison Gipstein & Hannah Lewis, Reassessing the Implications of Prior Restraint in the Digital Age as a Result of Ambiguity in New York Times Co. v. United States
  10. Kalel Charalambides, Engel v. Vitale and the Illusion of Voluntary Prayer: Religious Neutrality, Psychological Pressure, and the Impact on Students from All Academic, Social, and Cognitive Backgrounds
  11. Thomas Houghton & Evan Hernandez, The Alien Tort Statute and America's Betrayal of Universal Justice
  12. Emma Di Domenico, A Patchwork System: Why Consumer DNA Databases Require a Federal Framework for Privacy and Protection Interests
  13. Sophia O'Connor, Beyond Gideon: The Case for Counsel in Housing Court

Here's the introduction from the founder, Olivia Eve Gross:

It is with great pride that we at Studium introduce this year's edition of the National High School Law Review. Each volume reflects something larger than the collection of notes it contains. It represents a growing community of students and educators across the country who have committed themselves to studying constitutional law, engaging seriously with one another's ideas, and practicing the habits of thoughtful citizenship.

What began as a simple conviction, that students deserve the opportunity to wrestle directly with our nation's most consequential legal questions, has grown into a national movement. This year, we are especially proud to see that movement expanding into new schools, new states, and new classrooms, bringing thousands more students into conversations rooted in evidence, reason, and mutual respect.

The High School Law Review exists to give students an authentic place to think, write, and publish. Through close readings of Supreme Court opinions, sustained classroom discussion, and the publication of their own legal writing, students learn to analyze arguments with precision, communicate with clarity, and engage in constitutional reasoning while practicing agreeable disagreement. These are not simply academic skills. They are habits that prepare students to participate thoughtfully in civic life.

At the heart of this work is the practice of agreeable disagreement. Students are challenged not only to defend their own conclusions but also to understand the strongest versions of perspectives different from their own. They learn to separate ideas from identities, question their own assumptions, and recognize that disagreement, when approached with curiosity and generosity, strengthens rather than weakens a community of learners. The notes collected in this volume reflect that commitment. They demonstrate careful reasoning, genuine inquiry, and a willingness to engage difficult questions with both conviction and respect.

None of this would be possible without the extraordinary educators who make this work accessible to students in classrooms every day. Teachers create the conditions in which students are willing to ask difficult questions, revise their thinking, and engage one another with both rigor and kindness. Their leadership transforms constitutional law from a body of primary sources to be studied into a practice to be lived, and we remain deeply grateful for their partnership.

As our community continues to grow, so too does the significance of this publication. Students from across the country now contribute to a shared body of work, reading and learning from peers whose experiences, perspectives, and communities may differ greatly from their own. The National High School Law Review has become more than an annual publication; it is a national forum where young people discover that meaningful disagreement can be a source of learning rather than division.

To every student whose work appears in these pages, congratulations. Your willingness to think carefully, write thoughtfully, and share your ideas contributes to something much larger than a single legal note. To every teacher, school, and chapter that made this volume possible, thank you for believing in the importance of this work and for helping this community continue to grow.

We are excited by how far this movement has come and even more excited by where it is headed. We hope this edition inspires more schools to join us as we continue building a generation of citizens who know not only how to disagree, but how to do so with reason, respect, and an open mind.

The post Check Out the National High School Law Review, Vol. II appeared first on Reason.com.

articles.title: Today in Supreme Court History: August 22, 1998
articles.content:
1998年8月22日，巴里·布莱克（Barry Black）在弗吉尼亚州卡罗尔县组织了一次三K党（Ku Klux Klan）集会。2003年，弗吉尼亚州诉布莱克案（Virginia v. Black）中，最高法院审议了对其焚烧十字架行为的定罪是否合宪。该案涉及言论自由与种族仇恨行为的界限问题，成为宪法法理学的重要判例。

图片说明：伦昆斯特法院（The Rehnquist Court）
articles.summary:
8/22/1998: On August 22, 1998, Barry Black led a Ku Klux Klan rally in Carroll County, Virginia. The Supreme Court considered the constitutionality of his prosecution for cross burning in Virginia v. Black (2003).

articles.title: This Mamdani-Backed Bill Would Kill Jobs, Boost Unions, and Make Deliveries More Expensive
articles.content:
纽约市作为生活成本已极高的城市，若市议会通过新立法，可能使五区的包裹派送成本大幅增加。这项名为"快递安全法案"的议案，表面以提升安全为由，实则是工会加强自身影响力的障眼法。由纽约市议员泰菲·卡班于今年二月提出的议案，强制亚马逊、联邦快递等公司直接雇佣最后一英里派送员，而非依靠外包服务商。最后一英里派送——指包裹从物流中心到消费者门口的最终环节，因需频繁停车且高密度城市环境，向来为配送成本最高的部分。该立法恐将进一步推高这类派送的成本。

议案支持者包括市长佐赫兰·曼德尼，其主张亚马逊现行通过外包公司雇佣派送员的模式导致纽约市交通安全事故增加。依这理论，终结外包将降低员工流动率，并将责任直接转移至亚马逊，从而减少安全事故并更好保护派送员。然而，近年亚马逊已投入超120亿美元用于外包公司的安全技术升级，报告称自2020年起事故率下降48%。其中包括在布鲁克林建立的先进培训中心DNY7，为员工提供超越联邦最低要求的安全培训，并采购搭载摄像头的物流车及电动自行车等先进设备。

议案支持者援引亚马逊最后一英里外包公司员工伤亡率达每百人8.3次，远高于所有私营企业平均2.4次的数据。但这一对比毫无意义，真正相关的是全国配送员平均伤亡率8.0次，显示亚马逊外包公司已符合行业标准。

国际团结工会和纽约市中央劳工委员会（AFL-CIO）支持该议案。依联邦劳工法，亚马逊最后一英里外包合作伙伴虽可单独组工，但劳动合同并非与亚马逊直接签订。禁止外包将迫使亚马逊直接雇佣派送员，便于工会组织。

律师亚历克斯·麦克唐纳指出，这是工会近年新战术——若无法通过"基层组织运动"，便通过游说如本议案般"规避组织程序"的立法获得权力。换言之，无法通过集体谈判获得的权益，转而通过监管实现。

然而此类立法及纽约市的最后一英里外包禁止法案，或已被《国家劳工关系法》（NLRA）所限制。麦克唐纳认为，该法设计为"重叠权利、义务及自助区域"的体系，构建全国统一的劳工规则，强调"私下谈判与市场力量自由发挥"。若进步阵营及工会继续侵蚀这精心设计的架构，终将导致其彻底崩溃。

讽刺的是，该议案受害者反成支持者——上百名最后一英里派送员惊现市议会听证会，长达七小时的听证中他们站出来反对议案，其平均时薪24美元，并享有雇主资助的医保。亚马逊证词显示，其40家左右外包公司体现纽约城市多样性，其中25%为黑裔或西班牙裔拥有，10%为退伍军人经营。若议案通过，这些小企业将面临破产。

亚马逊警告，议案通过可能淘汰五区5000个工作岗位，因公司或需将配送中心迁至纽约以外地区。最保守估计，将减少在纽约建设最后一英里配送设施的动力，转而投向周边郡县或州，并加速自动化进程。

另一可能是纽约市民将见证更多"监管回应费"，类似Instacart因纽约市最低工资法实施后添加的5.99美元附加费。曼德尼支持的终结最后一英里外包，表面以安全为由，实则鼓励工会壮大、淘汰就业机会并推升配送成本，此荒谬法案应被存回仓库。

（原文最新更新日期：2024年3月21日）
articles.summary:
As if New York City weren't already an expensive enough place to live, legislation introduced to the City Council could soon make delivering packages in the five boroughs far costlier. Cloaked in the language of improving safety, the bill—recently endorsed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani—is little more than a thinly veiled attempt to strengthen the power of unions.

Introduced by NYC Council Member Tiffany Cabán in February, the misleadingly named "Delivery Protection Act" would require companies like Amazon and FedEx to directly hire employees for last-mile delivery, rather than contracting this service out to subcontractors. Last-mile delivery, which constitutes the final steps a package takes before hitting a consumer's doorstep, is the most expensive part of the delivery process, since it requires drivers to stop at many homes, often amid dense urban environments. The proposed legislation will only make this type of package delivery more expensive.

One of the main rationales behind the bill is safety. Proponents like Mamdani argue that Amazon's last-mile delivery service—which relies on subcontractor companies that hire their own workers—exacerbates traffic safety incidents in the Big Apple. Under this theory, ending the use of subcontractors would result in lower staff turnover and shift liability directly onto Amazon, which in turn could lower safety incidents and better protect the drivers themselves from injury.

But in recent years, Amazon has invested over $12 billion in technology and safety features for its delivery contractors, which it reports has led to a 48 percent decline in accident rates since 2020. This includes the creation of "DNY7"—a state-of-the-art Amazon training facility in Brooklyn where worker onboarding goes beyond federally mandated safety training—and through the acquisition of camera-equipped vans and modern electric bikes.

While proponents of the bill have pointed to statistics showing that the worker injury rates of Amazon's last-mile subcontractors is 8.3 per 100 workers versus 2.4 for all private employers, this comparison is essentially meaningless. The relevant comparison would be the national injury rate average for couriers—which is 8.0, suggesting that the Amazon's last-mile subcontractors are in line with industry norms.

The International Brotherhood of Teamsters and the New York City Central Labor Council, AFL-CIO are backing the bill. Under federal labor law, Amazon's subcontracted last-mile delivery partners can be individually unionized, but the labor contract wouldn't be signed with Amazon itself. Banning subcontracting for last-mile delivery would force Amazon to hire these deliverers as direct employees, making them easier to organize.

As attorney Alex MacDonald has noted, this is part of a larger strategy being employed by unions in recent years: If they are unable to organize through "organic, boots-on-the-ground campaigns," they now lobby for laws like this one that "read like a shortcut to organizing." In other words, what can't be accomplished by collective bargaining is pursued through direct regulation.

But these types of laws generally—and NYC's proposed ban on last-mile delivery services specifically—are arguably preempted by the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA). As MacDonald argues, the NLRA was designed to be a "scheme of overlapping rights, obligations, and zones of self-help" that create a cohesive national labor code—one which emphasizes "private negotiation and the free play of market forces." The more that progressive locales and labor unions undercut this carefully calibrated scaffolding, the wobblier it gets, until it is eventually undermined completely.

Ironically, NYC's last-mile delivery bill is also being opposed by those it purports to help: The City Council hearing stretched to seven hours long as several hundred last-mile delivery workers unexpectedly showed up to testify against it. These workers make around $24 per hour on average and have employer-funded healthcare through the subcontracted companies.

Amazon's last-mile subcontractors are also something else: small businesses. These 40 or so businesses represent a cross-section of New York City itself, with 25 percent operated by black or Hispanic owners, while another 10 percent are veteran-owned, according to testimony from Amazon. If the legislation passes, these businesses would be destroyed.

Amazon has also testified that the bill's passage could eliminate an estimated 5,000 jobs within the five boroughs, as the company warns it may need to relocate delivery operations outside of New York. At the very least, the effect will be to disincentivize the creation of further last-mile facilities in the city—in favor of neighboring counties or states—and further increase automation.

Another possibility is that New Yorkers will see yet more "regulatory response fees" tacked onto deliveries (or to Amazon Prime memberships), similar to Instacart's $5.99 surcharge that was introduced in response to NYC's recent minimum wage law for grocery delivery.

The Mamdani-backed effort to end last-mile delivery subcontracting in New York City is supposedly about safety. In reality, it will mostly serve to boost unions, eliminate jobs, and raise the cost of package delivery. It's an idea that deserves to be sent back to the warehouse.

The post This Mamdani-Backed Bill Would Kill Jobs, Boost Unions, and Make Deliveries More Expensive appeared first on Reason.com.

articles.title: Harry and Meghan's Security Problem Is Really a Gun-Control Problem
articles.content:
哈里王子和他的美国妻子梅根·马克尔据称将搬回英国，此前他们在美生活了逾六年。此次回归已引发关于他与王室裂痕、孩子阿奇王子和莉莉贝特公主是否能与查尔斯国王多相聚，以及具体搬家原因的讨论，但有一个被忽略的议题：英国的枪支法规。

这一决定确实出人意料，特别是哈里曾明确表示因安全原因不会返回英国。"我无法想象带着妻子和孩子在此时回到英国"，哈里去年在BBC的一次情绪化采访中表示。"看看风险，看看威胁，看看影响。如果我、我妻子或父亲的孙子（孙女）有任何三长两短——责任在哪里？所以这份护理义务已经被完全抛诸脑后。"

安全问题是哈里和梅根2020年离开英国的核心原因。退出王室并退出公职后，这对夫妇失去了公共资助的安保特权。哈里随后申请司法复核英国内政部剥夺其安保的决定，甚至愿意自掏腰包，不让纳税人买单。但申请被拒，迫使家庭搬往美国。

这次回归重新引发了对其安全的讨论，也必然引发为什么不能自资私人武装保安的问题。

1968年《枪支法》将枪支纳入严格的执照体系，而大多数手枪被完全禁止。这意味着合法持枪极其有限。如果你住在乡村，获得猎枪执照是可能的，步枪等其他枪支可用于获批的用途，如狩猎、灭害和射击。最新数据显示，英格兰和威尔士约50万人（不到1%人口）持有枪支或猎枪证书。

政府明确拒绝承认自卫是持枪的合法理由。"长期以来，连续多届政府认为私人持有和携带枪支用于个人保护很可能导致暴力水平上升。"政府指南说，"这一原则应适用于银行、保管珍贵物品或大量金钱的公司代表，或私人保安和保镖的申请。" 更离谱的是，胡椒喷雾也被视为武器，遭到《枪支法》完全禁止。

英国对枪支的抵触之深甚至连警察多数都不配枪。英格兰和威尔士仅4%的警员是操作现役枪支警员。当然，这些警员只用于应对最严重的犯罪，比如喜剧演员开玩笑。

哈里和梅根困境的核心是一个法律体系禁止私人武装保安。而在美国，私人武装保安是合法的，甚至是一个庞大的产业。全美有128万保安，根据法律，许多可合法持枪执勤。但在英国，自卫不是合法获枪理由，就连美国联邦调查局特工也需获得政府特殊许可才能携带。

尽管对哈里和梅根在英国的整体待遇存在怀疑，但在安全问题上，他们的担忧不无道理。哈里可以雇佣私人保安，但这些保安不仅无法获取情报——英国法律还禁止他们携带枪支，无法提供相应的武装保护。

这个问题超出了王室范畴。如果个人面临可信威胁，并愿意支付高水平、经过严格审查的私人保安费用，政府为何要阻止？像美国一样，英国也应允许安全市场的形成。英国政府无需让纳税人为哈里和梅根的安全买单，但也不应垄断他们能购买的保护类型。

（本文最初发表于Reason.com）
articles.summary:
Prince Harry and his American wife Meghan Markle are reportedly moving back to the United Kingdom after living in the United States for over six years. While the return has already sparked conversations about their rift with the royal family, whether their children Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet will be able to spend more time with King Charles, and the exact reasons for the move, there is one aspect of the conversation that has gone overlooked: British gun laws.

Their decision to return to the U.K. is certainly a surprise, especially because Prince Harry himself said that they would not be returning for security reasons.

"I can't see a world in which I'd be bringing my wife and children back to the U.K. at this point," Harry told the BBC in an emotional interview last year. "Look at the risks. Look at the threat. Look at the impact. If anything was to happen to me, my wife or my father's grandchildren—if anything was to happen to them—look where the responsibility lies, you know? So there's a duty of care that has been completely thrown out the window," Harry told the BBC.

Safety concerns were a central reason for Harry and Meghan's decision to leave Britain in 2020. After leaving the royal family and stepping back from official responsibilities, the couple lost their publicly funded security privileges. Harry subsequently filed a request for a judicial review of the U.K. Home Office's decision to take away their security. He even offered to pay for the security himself, so that it would not be at the expense of the taxpayer. The request was denied, prompting the family to move to the United States.

Their return reopens the debate about their security, and it certainly raises the question of why they cannot simply fund their own private armed security.

The Firearms Act 1968 subjects firearms to a strict licensing regime, while most handguns are entirely prohibited. In practice, this means that legal gun access is limited. If you live in the countryside, obtaining a shotgun license is doable, and rifles and other firearms can be licensed for approved purposes, such as hunting, pest control, and target shooting. According to the most recent data, just over half a million people in England and Wales—less than 1 percent of the population—hold a firearm or shotgun certificate.

One thing the government explicitly refuses to recognize as a legitimate reason for possessing a firearm is self-defense. "It has been the view of successive Governments for many years that the private possession and carriage of firearms for personal protection is likely to lead to an increase in levels of violence," reads the government's guide. "This principle should be maintained in the case of applications from representatives of banks and firms protecting valuables or large quantities of money, or from private security guards and bodyguards." Bizarrely, this includes pepper spray, which the Firearms Act categorizes as a weapon and entirely prohibits.

Britain is unusual enough in its aversion to firearms that even its police are overwhelmingly unarmed. Just 4 percent of officers in England and Wales are operationally deployable firearms officers. Of course, these police officers are only deployed to deal with the most serious of crimes, such as a comedian making a joke.

At the heart of Harry and Meghan's woes is a dispute over a legal system which prohibits private armed security. In the U.S., private armed security is legal and is an enormous industry in itself. More than 1.28 million security guards work across America and, subject to the law, many can legally work armed. In Britain, self-defense is not a legally permitted reason to obtain a firearm, and even American FBI agents must get special permission from the government to carry.

There are plenty of reasons to be skeptical of Harry and Meghan's complaints about their overall treatment in Britain, but on security, they do have a reason to be concerned. Harry can hire private security, but those guards not only lack access to intelligence—British law prevents those guards from carrying the firearms that would allow them to provide comparable armed protection.

The question raised is bigger than the royal family. If an individual faces a credible threat and is willing to pay for highly trained, vetted private security, why should the government prevent them from doing so? Like America, Britain ought to allow the creation of a security market. The U.K. does not have to make taxpayers foot the bill for Harry and Meghan's security, but neither should it maintain a monopoly on the kind of protection they are allowed to buy.
